FAQ

What does it mean that my genome sequencing failed?

  • Sequencing failure is defined as:
    • A high-quality assembly was not able to generated from your data
    • And the raw data target of 210 Mb (standard Bacteria service) or 360 Mb (Big Bacteria service) was not achieved
  • The raw sequencing reads (.fastq files) are including in the associated files
  • You may also still receive some of the other file types depending on at what stage your sample failed

Why did my genome sequencing fail?

  • Although we cannot provide definitive reasons on why each specific sample had poor data yield, the most common reasons include:
    • Your sample was not shipped at the required DNA concentration of 50 ng/µL
      • DNA quantification via Nanodrop is unreliable
      • Qubit (or equivalent fluorometric assay) is strongly recommended
    • Your sample was not from a bacterial isolate
    • Your sample contains fragmented/degraded gDNA – samples should be handled with utmost care, including:
      • Pipette with wide-bore tips
      • Minimize freeze/thaw cycles
      • Do not expose to extreme temperature/pH
      • Do not expose to UV radiation
      • Do not use intercalating dyes
      • Do not over-dry DNA pellet
      • Do not vortex
    • Your sample contains inhibitors, such as:
      • RNA
      • Detergents (SDS, Triton-X100, etc.)
      • Denaturants (guanidinium salts, phenol, etc.)
      • Residual contaminants from the organism/tissue (heme, humic acid, polyphenols, polysaccharides, lipids, etc.)
      • Insoluble, colored, or cloudy material
      • Other inhibitors (EDTA, etc.)
  • To prevent future failures, please adhere closely to our sample prep guidelines

What happens now?

  • If this is your first failure report, we will:
    1. Perform QC on your sample
    2. Adjust the prep protocol (e.g. clean up the sample, alter the prep input, etc.)
    3. Repeat the sequencing at no additional charge
    4. Combine the data from the two runs together to increase chances of a successful assembly
  • If the sample does not produce an assembly on the second attempt, we determine that your sample is not sequenceable, very likely due to one or more of the reasons listed above

How is the assembly generated?

  1. Remove the bottom 5% worst fastq reads via Filtlong v0.2.1 (default parameters)

  2. Downsample the reads to 250 Mb via Filtlong to create a rough sketch of the assembly with Miniasm v0.3

  3. Using information acquired from the Miniasm assembly, re-downsample the reads to ~100x coverage (do nothing if there isn’t at least 100x coverage) with heavy weight applied to removing low quality reads (helps small plasmids stick around)

  4. Run a Flye v2.9.1 assembly with parameters selected for high quality ONT reads

  5. Polish Flye assembly via Medaka v1.8.0 using the reads generated in step 3

  6. Run several analyses:

    • annotation
      • Bakta v1.11
    • contig analysis
      • Bandage v0.8.1
    • genome completeness and contamination
      • CheckM v1.2.2
    • species / plasmid identification
      • Mash v2.3 against RefSeq genomes+plasmids
      • Sourmash v4.6.1 against GenBank
      • CheckM v1.2.2
